objection: Does ‘firstborn of creation’ mean Jesus was created?
answer:
That's a really good question to ask before talking with your friends — this exact verse trips up a lot of careful readers, because "firstborn" in English does sound like "first one made." But in Scripture, "firstborn" (Greek *prototokos*) is regularly a title of rank and inheritance rather than a statement about birth order. Psalm 89:27 calls David God's "firstborn" even though David was neither God's literal son nor first in any chronological sense — the word marks him as preeminent heir, not as having "come into being" as God's son at some point.

Colossians 1:15 works the same way, and Paul makes sure we don't miss it: the very next verse says "for by Him were all things created" (Colossians 1:16). Read the logic carefully — if Christ is the one *through whom* all things were made, He cannot Himself be one of the "all things" that were made. That would be self-contradictory, like saying the carpenter is also one of the chairs he built. So "firstborn of all creation" means Christ holds the position of supreme heir and sovereign over creation, standing on the Creator's side of the line, not the first item within it.

You can see the same pattern in Revelation 3:14, where Christ is called "the beginning of the creation of God" — the word *arche* there carries the sense of source or origin, not "first thing originated." Read alongside John 1:3 and Colossians 1:16, the whole New Testament witness places Jesus consistently as the one through whom all things came to be, never as one among the things made.
